questions.question: What does GRC mean in an enterprise context?
questions.preferred_answer: GRC integrates governance, risk management, and compliance so objectives, decisions, controls, evidence, and accountability are managed coherently rather than through isolated functions.

source.title: ISACA - COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology

questions.question: How are governance and management different?
questions.preferred_answer: Governance evaluates stakeholder needs, sets direction, and monitors outcomes. Management plans, builds, runs, and monitors activities to achieve the direction established by the governing body.

source.title: ISACA - COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology

questions.question: What is enterprise governance of information and technology?
questions.preferred_answer: It is the system by which enterprise information and technology are directed and controlled to support value delivery, risk optimization, resource optimization, and strategic alignment.

source.title: ISACA - COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology

questions.question: What is the purpose of a governance framework?
questions.preferred_answer: A governance framework establishes decision rights, accountability, oversight, objectives, policies, performance measures, and escalation paths so activities remain aligned with enterprise goals.

source.title: ISACA - COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology

questions.question: What is the Three Lines Model?
questions.preferred_answer: The governing body is accountable for oversight; management owns and manages risk through first- and second-line roles; internal audit provides independent assurance as the third line.

source.title: The IIA - Three Lines Model

questions.question: Who owns risk in an organization?
questions.preferred_answer: Management and business process owners own risk. Risk, compliance, and security functions advise and monitor, while internal audit independently evaluates governance, risk management, and controls.

source.title: The IIA - Three Lines Model

questions.question: What is a policy hierarchy?
questions.preferred_answer: A policy hierarchy connects board or executive policy to standards, processes, procedures, guidelines, and evidence. Lower-level documents operationalize mandatory intent without contradicting higher-level requirements.

source.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 - Information Security Management Systems

questions.question: What makes a policy effective?
questions.preferred_answer: An effective policy has clear purpose, scope, authority, ownership, mandatory statements, defined exceptions, review frequency, communication, enforcement, and evidence that it is used.

source.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 - Information Security Management Systems

questions.question: What is governance by design?
questions.preferred_answer: Governance by design embeds ownership, approvals, segregation, monitoring, records, and escalation into processes and systems instead of adding compliance checks after implementation.

source.title: ISACA - COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology

questions.question: What is a governance committee expected to do?
questions.preferred_answer: It should make or oversee defined decisions, review risk and performance information, resolve cross-functional conflicts, approve exceptions, and track actions to closure.

source.title: ISACA - COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology

questions.question: What is organizational accountability?
questions.preferred_answer: Accountability means an identified role is answerable for an outcome, has sufficient authority and resources, and must explain decisions, performance, and unresolved risks.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.question: Why are decision rights important in GRC?
questions.preferred_answer: Decision rights specify who may approve, accept risk, grant exceptions, change controls, and escalate issues, reducing ambiguity and unauthorized commitments.

source.title: ISACA - COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology

questions.question: What is a governance operating model?
questions.preferred_answer: It defines bodies, roles, decision forums, processes, information flows, metrics, technology, and assurance relationships used to govern the organization.

source.title: ISACA - COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology

questions.question: How should GRC support business value rather than only compliance?
questions.preferred_answer: GRC should connect controls and obligations to business objectives, prioritize material risks, simplify duplicated requirements, and provide decision-ready information that enables responsible execution.

source.title: COSO - Enterprise Risk Management

questions.question: What is tone at the top?
questions.preferred_answer: Tone at the top is the behavior and messaging of leaders that shapes ethics, control discipline, transparency, and willingness to report problems. It must be reinforced by incentives and consequences.

source.title: COSO - Internal Control Integrated Framework

questions.question: How would you assess governance maturity?
questions.preferred_answer: Assess whether governance objectives, roles, forums, information, decisions, controls, and outcomes are defined, consistently performed, measured, improved, and supported by evidence.

source.title: ISACA - COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology

questions.question: What is risk?
questions.preferred_answer: Risk is the effect of uncertainty on objectives. In practice, describe the event or condition, affected objective, causes, consequences, and uncertainty rather than using a vague label.

source.title: ISO 31000 - Risk Management

questions.question: What is the difference between inherent and residual risk?
questions.preferred_answer: Inherent risk is exposure before considering controls; residual risk is exposure remaining after controls and other responses. Both should use stated assumptions and the same risk criteria.

source.title: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 - Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments

questions.question: What is risk appetite?
questions.preferred_answer: Risk appetite is the amount and type of risk an organization is willing to pursue or retain while achieving objectives. It guides boundaries, investment, and escalation.

source.title: COSO - Enterprise Risk Management

questions.question: How does risk tolerance differ from risk appetite?
questions.preferred_answer: Appetite is broad strategic willingness to accept risk; tolerance translates it into measurable variation or limits for specific objectives, processes, or risk indicators.

source.title: COSO - Enterprise Risk Management

questions.question: What are threat, vulnerability, likelihood, and impact?
questions.preferred_answer: A threat can exploit a vulnerability and cause harm. Likelihood estimates the chance of occurrence; impact estimates consequences to objectives, operations, assets, people, or obligations.

source.title: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 - Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments

questions.question: What makes a good risk statement?
questions.preferred_answer: A good statement uses cause-event-impact logic, names the objective at risk, avoids embedding the control as the risk, and is specific enough to assign ownership and treatment.

source.title: ISO 31000 - Risk Management

questions.question: What should a risk register contain?
questions.preferred_answer: It should record risk statements, owners, assets or processes, causes, impacts, ratings, controls, treatment actions, due dates, indicators, status, dependencies, and acceptance decisions.

source.title: NIST SP 800-39 - Managing Information Security Risk

questions.question: How should risk be scored?
questions.preferred_answer: Use defined, repeatable criteria for likelihood and impact, document assumptions, consider multiple impact dimensions, and avoid false precision. Escalation should not depend on arithmetic alone.

source.title: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 - Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments

questions.question: What is qualitative versus quantitative risk analysis?
questions.preferred_answer: Qualitative analysis uses defined categories and expert judgment; quantitative analysis uses numerical distributions, frequencies, and loss estimates. The method should match decision needs and data quality.

source.title: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 - Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments

questions.question: What are risk response options?
questions.preferred_answer: Common responses are avoid, reduce or mitigate, transfer or share, accept, and sometimes pursue or increase risk for opportunity. Each requires an owner and decision authority.

source.title: ISO 31000 - Risk Management

questions.question: When is risk acceptance valid?
questions.preferred_answer: Acceptance is valid when an authorized owner understands residual exposure, alternatives, duration, conditions, monitoring, and obligations, and records the decision within appetite.

source.title: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 - Risk Management Framework

questions.question: What is a key risk indicator?
questions.preferred_answer: A KRI is a measurable signal of changing exposure or control conditions. It needs a threshold, owner, data source, frequency, response, and relationship to a defined risk.

source.title: COSO - Enterprise Risk Management

questions.question: How do risk assessments become stale?
questions.preferred_answer: They become stale when assets, threats, dependencies, regulations, controls, or business objectives change but the assessment is not updated. Trigger-based reviews complement periodic reviews.

source.title: NIST SP 800-39 - Managing Information Security Risk

questions.question: What is risk aggregation?
questions.preferred_answer: Risk aggregation combines related exposures and dependencies to show enterprise-level concentration or cumulative impact without simply adding incompatible scores.

source.title: COSO - Enterprise Risk Management

questions.question: How should cyber risk connect to enterprise risk management?
questions.preferred_answer: Translate cyber scenarios into business objectives, financial and operational impacts, appetite, ownership, and portfolio decisions so cyber risk is governed with other enterprise risks.

source.title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0

questions.question: What is continuous risk monitoring?
questions.preferred_answer: It is ongoing collection and review of risk, control, threat, and business-change information to identify material changes and trigger reassessment or action.

source.title: NIST SP 800-137 - Information Security Continuous Monitoring

questions.question: What is an internal control?
questions.preferred_answer: An internal control is an action or mechanism designed to provide reasonable assurance that objectives are achieved and risks are managed within acceptable limits.

source.title: COSO - Internal Control Integrated Framework

questions.question: What are preventive, detective, and corrective controls?
questions.preferred_answer: Preventive controls reduce the chance of an event; detective controls identify events or deviations; corrective controls restore conditions, remediate causes, or limit consequences.

source.title: COSO - Internal Control Integrated Framework

questions.question: What is a key control?
questions.preferred_answer: A key control is one whose failure could materially affect an objective or leave a significant risk insufficiently addressed. Key status should be justified, not inherited from a template.

source.title: COSO - Internal Control Integrated Framework

questions.question: What is control design effectiveness?
questions.preferred_answer: Design effectiveness asks whether the control, if performed as intended by competent people with appropriate authority, could prevent or detect the relevant risk in time.

source.title: PCAOB AS 2201 - Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

questions.question: What is operating effectiveness?
questions.preferred_answer: Operating effectiveness asks whether the control actually operated as designed, consistently, by authorized and competent performers, throughout the relevant period.

source.title: PCAOB AS 2201 - Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

questions.question: What is a compensating control?
questions.preferred_answer: A compensating control provides equivalent risk reduction when the primary requirement cannot be met. It must address the same objective and be formally justified, tested, and monitored.

source.title: PCI Security Standards Council - PCI DSS v4.0.1

questions.question: What is a control objective?
questions.preferred_answer: A control objective states the desired outcome that controls are intended to achieve. It should be risk-linked, testable, and technology-neutral where possible.

source.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 - Security and Privacy Controls

questions.question: How do manual and automated controls differ?
questions.preferred_answer: Manual controls depend mainly on human performance; automated controls are executed by systems. IT-dependent manual controls rely on reports or configurations and require testing of those dependencies.

source.title: PCAOB AS 2201 - Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

questions.question: What is a control matrix?
questions.preferred_answer: A risk and control matrix links objectives and risks to controls, owners, frequency, evidence, assertions, systems, testing steps, results, deficiencies, and remediation.

source.title: ISACA - IT Audit Resources and ITAF

questions.question: Why map controls across frameworks?
questions.preferred_answer: Mapping identifies common objectives, reduces duplicated evidence requests, supports compliance reuse, and reveals gaps. Mapping should not assume differently worded requirements are automatically equivalent.

source.title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0

questions.question: What is a common control?
questions.preferred_answer: A common control is implemented once and inherited by multiple systems or processes. The provider defines scope, operation, evidence, responsibilities, and conditions of inheritance.

source.title: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 - Risk Management Framework

questions.question: What is control ownership?
questions.preferred_answer: The control owner is accountable for design, documentation, operation, evidence, performance, issue response, and change impact, even when execution is delegated.

source.title: COSO - Internal Control Integrated Framework

questions.question: How should control frequency be selected?
questions.preferred_answer: Frequency should reflect risk velocity, transaction volume, detection window, dependency on other controls, legal requirements, and the time available to prevent material harm.

source.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 - Security and Privacy Controls

questions.question: What is a control baseline?
questions.preferred_answer: A baseline is a selected starting set of controls tailored to system impact, environment, threats, obligations, and organizational requirements. It is not a substitute for risk analysis.

source.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 - Security and Privacy Controls

questions.question: How do you prevent control proliferation?
questions.preferred_answer: Use a normalized control library, map multiple requirements to shared objectives, remove duplicates, assign authoritative ownership, and retain only controls that address defined risks or obligations.

source.title: ISACA - COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology

questions.question: What evidence demonstrates a control is sustainable?
questions.preferred_answer: Sustainable evidence includes clear ownership, repeatable procedures, reliable data, retained records, exception handling, monitoring, training, capacity, and integration with change management.

source.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 - Information Security Management Systems

questions.question: What is the purpose of internal auditing?
questions.preferred_answer: Internal auditing strengthens the organization through independent, risk-based assurance and advice on governance, risk management, and control processes.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.question: What is audit independence?
questions.preferred_answer: Independence is the freedom from conditions that threaten the internal audit function ability to perform responsibilities objectively, supported by appropriate organizational positioning and board access.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.question: What is auditor objectivity?
questions.preferred_answer: Objectivity is an unbiased mental attitude that enables auditors to make balanced judgments without subordinating conclusions to others or conflicts of interest.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.question: What is reasonable assurance?
questions.preferred_answer: Reasonable assurance is a high but not absolute level of confidence because controls and audits face limitations such as judgment, sampling, collusion, change, and cost.

source.title: COSO - Internal Control Integrated Framework

questions.question: What is an assurance engagement?
questions.preferred_answer: An assurance engagement independently evaluates evidence against criteria and communicates a conclusion about governance, risk, controls, or performance.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.question: What is an advisory engagement?
questions.preferred_answer: An advisory engagement provides advice, facilitation, training, or insight without assuming management responsibility. Scope and independence safeguards should be agreed.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.question: What is due professional care?
questions.preferred_answer: It is the diligence, judgment, skepticism, competence, and attention expected from a prudent auditor, considering complexity, materiality, fraud risk, and evidence quality.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.question: What is professional skepticism?
questions.preferred_answer: Professional skepticism is a questioning mindset that critically evaluates evidence, contradictory information, management bias, and the possibility of error or fraud.

source.title: ISACA - IT Audit Resources and ITAF

questions.question: What is an audit charter?
questions.preferred_answer: The charter formally defines internal audit purpose, authority, responsibility, independence, access rights, scope, and relationship with the board and management.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.question: What is a risk-based audit plan?
questions.preferred_answer: It prioritizes assurance work based on enterprise objectives, risk exposure, change, prior findings, regulatory needs, coverage gaps, and available resources, with dynamic updates.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.question: How does ITAF relate to IT audit?
questions.preferred_answer: ITAF provides standards, guidance, and techniques for planning, performing, reporting, and following up IT audit and assurance engagements.

source.title: ISACA - IT Audit Resources and ITAF

questions.question: What is the difference between internal and external audit?
questions.preferred_answer: Internal audit provides broad assurance and advice for the organization; external audit primarily expresses opinions required by external stakeholders, often on financial statements and related controls.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.question: When can internal audit rely on other assurance providers?
questions.preferred_answer: Reliance is appropriate after assessing the provider mandate, independence, competence, methodology, scope, evidence quality, results, and whether work addresses the audit objective.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.question: What is a quality assurance and improvement program?
questions.preferred_answer: A QAIP evaluates conformance, efficiency, stakeholder value, and improvement of internal audit through ongoing monitoring and periodic internal and external assessments.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.question: How should auditors handle conflicts of interest?
questions.preferred_answer: Disclose the conflict promptly, avoid or modify the assignment, apply safeguards, and document the decision so objectivity is protected and transparent.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.question: What is audit universe?
questions.preferred_answer: The audit universe is the structured inventory of auditable entities, processes, systems, risks, programs, legal entities, and third parties used to plan coverage.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.category: 5. IT Audit Planning, Scoping and Materiality
questions.question: What is an audit objective?
questions.preferred_answer: An audit objective states what the engagement will determine or evaluate and should be linked to risk, stakeholder needs, and measurable criteria.

source.title: ISACA - IT Audit Resources and ITAF

questions.category: 5. IT Audit Planning, Scoping and Materiality
questions.question: How is audit scope defined?
questions.preferred_answer: Scope defines entities, locations, systems, processes, time period, control domains, interfaces, exclusions, and dependencies necessary to achieve the objective.

source.title: ISACA - IT Audit Resources and ITAF

questions.category: 5. IT Audit Planning, Scoping and Materiality
questions.question: What is materiality in an IT audit?
questions.preferred_answer: Materiality is the significance of an issue to decisions or objectives, considering financial, operational, regulatory, security, privacy, customer, and reputational consequences.

source.title: PCAOB AS 2201 - Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

questions.category: 5. IT Audit Planning, Scoping and Materiality
questions.question: What is a preliminary risk assessment?
questions.preferred_answer: It identifies objectives, changes, assets, dependencies, threats, prior issues, regulations, and control concerns to focus scope, resources, and testing.

source.title: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 - Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments

questions.category: 5. IT Audit Planning, Scoping and Materiality
questions.question: Why perform a process walkthrough?
questions.preferred_answer: A walkthrough validates understanding from initiation to recording and reporting, identifies systems and handoffs, confirms control placement, and exposes differences between documentation and practice.

source.title: PCAOB AS 2201 - Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

questions.category: 5. IT Audit Planning, Scoping and Materiality
questions.question: What should be included in an audit planning memo?
questions.preferred_answer: Include background, objective, scope, risks, criteria, systems, locations, stakeholders, approach, sampling, resources, schedule, dependencies, communication, and limitations.

source.title: ISACA - IT Audit Resources and ITAF

questions.category: 5. IT Audit Planning, Scoping and Materiality
questions.question: How do you select audit criteria?
questions.preferred_answer: Use authoritative laws, regulations, contracts, policies, standards, frameworks, approved designs, service commitments, and risk expectations that are relevant, reliable, and communicated.

source.title: ISO 19011 - Guidelines for Auditing Management Systems

questions.category: 5. IT Audit Planning, Scoping and Materiality
questions.question: What is an audit program?
questions.preferred_answer: An audit program translates objectives and risks into detailed procedures, evidence requirements, populations, sampling, responsibilities, timing, and review points.

source.title: ISACA - IT Audit Resources and ITAF

questions.category: 5. IT Audit Planning, Scoping and Materiality
questions.question: How should prior findings affect scope?
questions.preferred_answer: Evaluate remediation status, recurrence, root causes, compensating controls, and related risk. Prior findings may increase testing depth but should not replace current risk assessment.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.category: 5. IT Audit Planning, Scoping and Materiality
questions.question: How do system interfaces affect audit scope?
questions.preferred_answer: Interfaces can introduce completeness, accuracy, authorization, timing, transformation, and reconciliation risks, so source, transfer, error handling, and target controls may all require testing.

source.title: PCAOB AS 2201 - Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

questions.category: 5. IT Audit Planning, Scoping and Materiality
questions.question: How should cloud services be scoped?
questions.preferred_answer: Define service and deployment models, data and regions, tenant configuration, shared responsibilities, inherited controls, provider reports, subcontractors, integrations, and customer-managed controls.

source.title: Cloud Security Alliance - Cloud Controls Matrix

questions.category: 5. IT Audit Planning, Scoping and Materiality
questions.question: How do you scope a SOX ITGC audit?
questions.preferred_answer: Start from material financial reporting processes and systems, identify relevant applications, databases, infrastructure, interfaces, reports, and ITGCs that support automated and IT-dependent controls.

source.title: PCAOB AS 2201 - Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

questions.category: 5. IT Audit Planning, Scoping and Materiality
questions.question: What is a scope limitation?
questions.preferred_answer: A scope limitation is a restriction that prevents sufficient work, such as denied access, unavailable evidence, time constraints, or excluded systems. Its effect must be evaluated and communicated.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.category: 5. IT Audit Planning, Scoping and Materiality
questions.question: How do you budget audit effort?
questions.preferred_answer: Estimate effort based on risk, complexity, locations, populations, specialist needs, data availability, coordination, review time, and contingency for exceptions.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.category: 5. IT Audit Planning, Scoping and Materiality
questions.question: What is an opening meeting for?
questions.preferred_answer: It confirms objective, scope, responsibilities, logistics, evidence channels, timelines, escalation, confidentiality, and expectations while allowing management to share context and changes.

source.title: ISO 19011 - Guidelines for Auditing Management Systems

questions.category: 5. IT Audit Planning, Scoping and Materiality
questions.question: When should an audit plan be changed?
questions.preferred_answer: Change it when new risks, incidents, acquisitions, control failures, regulatory deadlines, evidence limitations, or business changes materially affect objectives or planned coverage.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.question: What makes audit evidence sufficient and appropriate?
questions.preferred_answer: Sufficiency is the quantity of evidence; appropriateness is its relevance and reliability. Both depend on risk, source, method, consistency, and the strength of conclusions required.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.question: Which evidence is generally more reliable?
questions.preferred_answer: Evidence obtained directly by the auditor from independent sources or controlled systems is generally stronger than uncorroborated verbal explanations or manually prepared screenshots.

source.title: ISACA - IT Audit Resources and ITAF

questions.question: What is inquiry and why is it insufficient alone?
questions.preferred_answer: Inquiry asks knowledgeable people for information, but responses can be incomplete or biased. Corroborate with observation, inspection, reperformance, analytics, or external evidence.

source.title: ISO 19011 - Guidelines for Auditing Management Systems

questions.question: What is reperformance?
questions.preferred_answer: Reperformance independently executes a control or calculation using the same inputs and criteria to determine whether the expected result is produced.

source.title: ISACA - IT Audit Resources and ITAF

questions.question: What is inspection of evidence?
questions.preferred_answer: Inspection examines documents, records, configurations, logs, reports, tickets, approvals, or physical assets to verify occurrence, authorization, completeness, and consistency.

source.title: ISO 19011 - Guidelines for Auditing Management Systems

questions.question: What is observation as an audit technique?
questions.preferred_answer: Observation watches a process or control being performed. It is useful for understanding behavior but represents only the observed time and may influence participants.

source.title: ISO 19011 - Guidelines for Auditing Management Systems

questions.question: What is population completeness?
questions.preferred_answer: Population completeness means the dataset includes all relevant items for the period and criteria. Validate source, extraction logic, date boundaries, duplicates, reconciliations, and record counts.

source.title: PCAOB AS 2201 - Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

questions.question: How do statistical and non-statistical sampling differ?
questions.preferred_answer: Statistical sampling uses probability selection and quantified sampling risk; non-statistical sampling uses auditor judgment. Both require a defined population, selection method, and evaluation.

source.title: PCAOB AS 2201 - Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

questions.question: What is sampling risk?
questions.preferred_answer: Sampling risk is the chance that the selected sample leads to a different conclusion than testing the full population. Sample design should reflect expected deviation and tolerable risk.

source.title: PCAOB AS 2201 - Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

questions.question: How should exceptions be evaluated?
questions.preferred_answer: Confirm facts, determine whether the item is an error or control deviation, investigate cause and frequency, project implications where appropriate, and assess compensating controls and impact.

source.title: ISACA - IT Audit Resources and ITAF

questions.question: What is data analytics in auditing?
questions.preferred_answer: Audit analytics uses structured or unstructured data to test full populations, identify anomalies, stratify risk, validate controls, and support conclusions, while preserving reproducibility and data integrity.

source.title: ISACA - IT Audit Resources and ITAF

questions.question: What controls are needed over auditor-developed scripts?
questions.preferred_answer: Use version control, documented logic, test cases, peer review, source reconciliation, parameter checks, protected outputs, and retained execution evidence.

source.title: ISACA - IT Audit Resources and ITAF

questions.question: How do screenshots affect evidence quality?
questions.preferred_answer: Screenshots can show a point-in-time state but may lack provenance, completeness, timestamps, or hidden settings. Prefer exported configurations, logs, queries, or direct observation where possible.

source.title: ISACA - IT Audit Resources and ITAF

questions.question: What is chain of custody for audit evidence?
questions.preferred_answer: It documents who collected, accessed, transferred, stored, and changed evidence so authenticity, integrity, confidentiality, and admissibility can be demonstrated.

source.title: NIST SP 800-115 - Technical Guide to Security Testing and Assessment

questions.question: How should audit workpapers be structured?
questions.preferred_answer: Workpapers should show objective, procedure, population, selection, evidence, analysis, result, reviewer sign-off, cross-references, and a clear link from risk to conclusion.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.question: What is evidence retention?
questions.preferred_answer: Retention preserves records long enough to support conclusions, quality reviews, legal or regulatory needs, and follow-up, with controls for confidentiality, access, integrity, and disposal.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.question: What are IT general controls?
questions.preferred_answer: ITGCs are foundational controls over access, change, operations, development, security, and continuity that support reliable processing and application controls across systems.

source.title: PCAOB AS 2201 - Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

questions.question: Why do weak ITGCs affect automated controls?
questions.preferred_answer: Automated controls depend on systems, configurations, code, data, and access. Weak ITGCs reduce confidence that the automated control remained authorized, accurate, and unchanged.

source.title: PCAOB AS 2201 - Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

questions.question: What are common ITGC domains?
questions.preferred_answer: Common domains include logical access, privileged access, change management, computer operations, backup and recovery, job scheduling, incident management, development, and vendor management.

source.title: ISACA - COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology

questions.question: What is an ITGC control dependency?
questions.preferred_answer: A dependency is another control, system, report, or data source required for the control to work. Dependencies must be identified and tested when material.

source.title: PCAOB AS 2201 - Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

questions.question: How should batch job controls be tested?
questions.preferred_answer: Evaluate scheduling authorization, parameter protection, monitoring, failure alerts, restart procedures, output reconciliation, exception handling, and evidence across the period.

source.title: ISACA - COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology

questions.question: What is an interface control?
questions.preferred_answer: An interface control ensures data transferred between systems is complete, accurate, authorized, timely, and reconciled, with rejected items logged and resolved.

source.title: COSO - Internal Control Integrated Framework

questions.question: What are backup controls expected to cover?
questions.preferred_answer: They should define scope, frequency, encryption, retention, offsite or immutable copies, monitoring, failures, restoration testing, ownership, and alignment with recovery objectives.

source.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 - Contingency Planning Guide

questions.question: Why is restore testing more important than backup success logs?
questions.preferred_answer: A successful backup job only shows data was copied. Restore testing demonstrates usability, integrity, procedures, access, dependencies, timing, and the ability to meet recovery objectives.

source.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 - Contingency Planning Guide

questions.question: What is configuration management control?
questions.preferred_answer: It establishes approved baselines, secure settings, change authorization, version control, drift detection, exception management, and periodic review for technology assets.

source.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 - Security and Privacy Controls

questions.question: What is an end-user computing control?
questions.preferred_answer: EUC controls govern spreadsheets, scripts, databases, and user-developed tools through inventory, risk classification, access, change control, validation, backup, and independent review.

source.title: COSO - Internal Control Integrated Framework

questions.question: How should system-generated reports used in controls be audited?
questions.preferred_answer: Test report logic, parameters, source data, interfaces, access, change controls, completeness, accuracy, and whether the control performer reviews the correct output.

source.title: PCAOB AS 2201 - Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

questions.question: What is information produced by the entity (IPE)?
questions.preferred_answer: IPE is data, reports, or spreadsheets generated by the organization and used as audit evidence or in controls. Its completeness and accuracy must be established.

source.title: PCAOB AS 2201 - Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

questions.question: What operational controls support time synchronization?
questions.preferred_answer: Define authoritative time sources, redundant synchronization, secure configuration, drift monitoring, exception alerts, timezone handling, and review because accurate timestamps support logs and investigations.

source.title: CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1

questions.question: How are incident and problem records relevant to ITGC testing?
questions.preferred_answer: They reveal recurring failures, control bypasses, unauthorized changes, operational instability, unresolved root causes, and whether escalation and corrective actions are effective.

source.title: ISACA - COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology

questions.question: What is the role of service organization controls reports?
questions.preferred_answer: SOC reports may provide assurance over outsourced controls, but users must assess scope, period, opinion, exceptions, subservice organizations, complementary user controls, and bridge coverage.

source.title: AICPA & CIMA - SOC for Service Organizations

questions.question: How do you conclude on ITGC effectiveness?
questions.preferred_answer: Aggregate design and operating results, exceptions, compensating controls, dependencies, duration, pervasiveness, affected applications, and impact on planned reliance or substantive work.

source.title: PCAOB AS 2201 - Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

questions.question: What is least privilege?
questions.preferred_answer: Least privilege grants only the access needed for approved duties, at the minimum level and duration, with periodic validation and prompt removal.

source.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 - Security and Privacy Controls

questions.question: What is segregation of duties?
questions.preferred_answer: Segregation of duties divides incompatible responsibilities so one person cannot initiate, approve, execute, and conceal a sensitive transaction or change.

source.title: COSO - Internal Control Integrated Framework

questions.question: What is joiner-mover-leaver control?
questions.preferred_answer: JML controls create access from approved roles, update it when duties change, and revoke it promptly at termination, including accounts, tokens, groups, applications, and physical access.

source.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 - Security and Privacy Controls

questions.question: How should access requests be controlled?
questions.preferred_answer: Require verified identity, business justification, appropriate owner approval, role and SoD checks, least privilege, defined duration, logging, and evidence of provisioning.

source.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 - Security and Privacy Controls

questions.question: What is periodic access recertification?
questions.preferred_answer: It is a documented review by accountable owners to confirm users, privileges, roles, service accounts, and exceptions remain appropriate, followed by tracked removal of unnecessary access.

source.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 - Security and Privacy Controls

questions.question: What makes an access review ineffective?
questions.preferred_answer: Common failures include incomplete populations, unclear entitlements, rubber-stamp approval, inappropriate reviewers, no SoD context, excluded service accounts, and untracked revocation.

source.title: ISACA - IT Audit Resources and ITAF

questions.question: What are privileged access management controls?
questions.preferred_answer: PAM controls discover and vault privileged credentials, enforce approval and time limits, record sessions, rotate secrets, restrict paths, monitor activity, and review emergency use.

source.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 - Security and Privacy Controls

questions.question: What is a break-glass account?
questions.preferred_answer: A break-glass account provides emergency privileged access under strict conditions, with secured credentials, limited use, immediate alerts, complete logging, post-use review, and rotation.

source.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 - Security and Privacy Controls

questions.question: How should service accounts be governed?
questions.preferred_answer: Assign owners and purpose, prohibit interactive use where possible, use managed identities or vaulting, rotate credentials, restrict privileges, monitor activity, and review dependencies before changes.

source.title: CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1

questions.question: What is role-based access control?
questions.preferred_answer: RBAC assigns permissions to defined job or functional roles and users to roles. Good governance requires role ownership, lifecycle, SoD analysis, and avoidance of role explosion.

source.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 - Security and Privacy Controls

questions.question: What is attribute-based access control?
questions.preferred_answer: ABAC makes decisions using attributes of subjects, resources, actions, and environment. It is flexible but depends on reliable attributes, policy logic, governance, and testing.

source.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 - Security and Privacy Controls

questions.question: How should multi-factor authentication be audited?
questions.preferred_answer: Verify scope, factor strength, enrollment, recovery, exemptions, privileged and remote coverage, conditional access, logging, failure handling, and resistance to bypass.

source.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 - Security and Privacy Controls

questions.question: What is an orphan account?
questions.preferred_answer: An orphan account lacks a valid active owner or business purpose, often after termination, transfer, application change, or contractor departure, and creates unauthorized access risk.

source.title: CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1

questions.question: How do you test termination access removal?
questions.preferred_answer: Select terminated users from authoritative HR data, trace all relevant identities and entitlements, compare timestamps to policy, inspect exceptions, and verify privileged, remote, and physical access removal.

source.title: ISACA - IT Audit Resources and ITAF

questions.question: What controls apply to third-party access?
questions.preferred_answer: Use sponsor approval, contractual requirements, identity verification, least privilege, time limits, MFA, segmented access, monitoring, periodic review, and immediate revocation when the engagement ends.

source.title: NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1 - Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management

questions.question: How should access-control exceptions be managed?
questions.preferred_answer: Document the need, risk, compensating controls, owner, approver, duration, monitoring, review date, and removal plan. Permanent undocumented exceptions indicate control failure.

source.title: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 - Risk Management Framework

questions.question: What is the objective of change management control?
questions.preferred_answer: It ensures production changes are authorized, tested, traceable, segregated, scheduled, implemented, validated, and reversible so integrity and availability are protected.

source.title: ISACA - COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology

questions.question: What evidence should exist for a normal change?
questions.preferred_answer: Evidence should include request, business and technical justification, risk, approvals, testing, affected assets, implementation plan, communication, rollback, validation, and closure.

source.title: ISACA - COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology

questions.question: How should emergency changes be controlled?
questions.preferred_answer: Define genuine emergency criteria, restrict approvers and implementers, capture minimum pre-change evidence, test where feasible, monitor impact, and perform prompt retrospective review.

source.title: ISACA - COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology

questions.question: Why is developer access to production risky?
questions.preferred_answer: It can bypass independent approval, testing, and traceability. Where unavoidable, use time-bound privileged access, monitoring, ticket linkage, independent review, and rapid removal.

source.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 - Security and Privacy Controls

questions.question: What is source-code version control expected to provide?
questions.preferred_answer: It should provide identity, history, branches, approvals, protected repositories, integrity, rollback, issue linkage, and restricted changes to production-bound code.

source.title: NIST SP 800-218 - Secure Software Development Framework

questions.question: What are secure SDLC controls?
questions.preferred_answer: Secure SDLC integrates security requirements, threat modeling, approved components, code review, testing, vulnerability remediation, release approval, and post-release monitoring throughout development.

source.title: NIST SP 800-218 - Secure Software Development Framework

questions.question: What is application control?
questions.preferred_answer: An application control supports complete, accurate, authorized, valid, and timely processing within a business application, including input, processing, interface, and output controls.

source.title: COSO - Internal Control Integrated Framework

questions.question: What is input validation control?
questions.preferred_answer: It verifies submitted data format, range, completeness, authorization, reasonableness, and duplicates before processing, with rejected items logged and resolved.

source.title: OWASP Application Security Verification Standard

questions.question: What are automated calculations and configurations tested for?
questions.preferred_answer: Test approved logic, parameters, effective dates, access, changes, boundary conditions, source data, rounding, exceptions, and reconciliation to expected results.

source.title: PCAOB AS 2201 - Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

questions.question: What is a three-way match control?
questions.preferred_answer: It compares purchase order, receipt, and invoice data before payment, using defined tolerances and approval of exceptions to reduce invalid or inaccurate payments.

source.title: COSO - Internal Control Integrated Framework

questions.question: How should interface reconciliation work?
questions.preferred_answer: Compare record counts, totals, control fields, rejected transactions, duplicate detection, timing, and correction status between source and target systems.

source.title: COSO - Internal Control Integrated Framework

questions.question: What is user acceptance testing governance?
questions.preferred_answer: UAT should have representative business users, traceability to requirements and risks, controlled data, documented results, defect decisions, and accountable sign-off before release.

source.title: ISACA - COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology

questions.question: What is migration control?
questions.preferred_answer: Migration controls protect completeness, accuracy, security, and traceability through profiling, cleansing, mapping, test loads, reconciliations, approvals, cutover, rollback, and retention.

source.title: ISACA - COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology

questions.question: How should open-source component risk be governed?
questions.preferred_answer: Maintain an inventory and provenance, assess licenses and vulnerabilities, approve use, monitor dependencies, patch or replace components, and define response for unsupported libraries.

source.title: NIST SP 800-218 - Secure Software Development Framework

questions.question: What control concerns arise in CI/CD pipelines?
questions.preferred_answer: Review repository access, branch protection, build integrity, secrets, approvals, test gates, artifact signing, environment segregation, deployment rights, logs, and rollback.

source.title: NIST SP 800-218 - Secure Software Development Framework

questions.question: How do you test change-management operating effectiveness?
questions.preferred_answer: Select a complete change population, stratify by risk and type, test required attributes and evidence, inspect emergency changes and direct production activity, and evaluate exceptions across the period.

source.title: ISACA - IT Audit Resources and ITAF

questions.question: What is the shared responsibility model?
questions.preferred_answer: The provider secures defined cloud infrastructure and services while the customer secures its data, identities, configurations, workloads, and usage according to the service model. Responsibilities must be explicitly mapped.

source.title: AWS - Shared Responsibility Model

questions.question: How should cloud configuration be audited?
questions.preferred_answer: Use authoritative asset inventory, organization and account structure, identity, network exposure, encryption, logging, backup, guardrails, exceptions, and automated configuration evidence across environments.

source.title: Cloud Security Alliance - Cloud Controls Matrix

questions.question: What is cloud control inheritance?
questions.preferred_answer: Customers may inherit provider controls, but must validate the service, scope, assurance report, customer responsibilities, configuration conditions, and any gaps not covered by the provider.

source.title: FedRAMP - Authorization and Continuous Monitoring

questions.question: What is a security baseline audit?
questions.preferred_answer: It compares actual configurations to approved secure baselines, evaluates deviations and exceptions, and confirms remediation or risk acceptance using reliable automated and manual evidence.

source.title: CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1

questions.question: What should vulnerability-management controls include?
questions.preferred_answer: Asset coverage, authenticated scanning where appropriate, frequency, prioritization, ownership, remediation targets, exceptions, validation, threat context, and reporting of overdue exposure.

source.title: CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1

questions.question: How should penetration-test results be used in audit?
questions.preferred_answer: Assess scope, independence, methodology, limitations, findings, validation, remediation, and whether testing covers relevant attack paths; do not treat a clean report as complete assurance.

source.title: NIST SP 800-115 - Technical Guide to Security Testing and Assessment

questions.question: What is zero trust from an audit perspective?
questions.preferred_answer: Zero trust requires continuous, context-aware authorization for each access request, strong identity, least privilege, segmentation, telemetry, and policy enforcement rather than trust based on network location.

source.title: NIST SP 800-207 - Zero Trust Architecture

questions.question: What logging controls should be evaluated?
questions.preferred_answer: Evaluate required events, source coverage, integrity, time synchronization, centralization, access, retention, alerting, review, storage capacity, privacy, and response to logging failures.

source.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 - Security and Privacy Controls

questions.question: How do you audit security monitoring effectiveness?
questions.preferred_answer: Trace prioritized threats to data sources, detection logic, alert quality, coverage, triage, response, tuning, testing, staffing, and metrics such as detection and containment time.

source.title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0

questions.question: What is encryption key management control?
questions.preferred_answer: It governs key generation, ownership, storage, access, separation, rotation, backup, revocation, destruction, usage, and monitoring across the key lifecycle.

source.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 - Security and Privacy Controls

questions.question: How should endpoint security controls be audited?
questions.preferred_answer: Confirm inventory, approved agents, configuration, update health, tamper protection, alert coverage, exclusions, response integration, and treatment of unsupported or unmanaged endpoints.

source.title: CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1

questions.question: What is network segmentation control?
questions.preferred_answer: Segmentation limits communication and blast radius using defined zones, allowed flows, enforcement points, rule governance, testing, and monitoring of unauthorized paths.

source.title: PCI Security Standards Council - PCI DSS v4.0.1

questions.question: How should firewall rules be reviewed?
questions.preferred_answer: Evaluate business ownership, source and destination, ports, purpose, risk, approval, expiry, overly broad rules, shadowed rules, unused rules, and evidence of periodic recertification.

source.title: PCI Security Standards Council - PCI DSS v4.0.1

questions.question: What is secure-by-design evidence?
questions.preferred_answer: Evidence includes security requirements, threat modeling, safe defaults, reduced customer burden, vulnerability handling, product telemetry, and executive accountability throughout the product lifecycle.

source.title: CISA - Secure by Design

questions.question: How should cyber maturity be assessed?
questions.preferred_answer: Use defined outcomes and evidence across governance, identification, protection, detection, response, and recovery, while distinguishing capability, implementation, consistency, and measured effectiveness.

source.title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0

questions.question: What is continuous control monitoring in cybersecurity?
questions.preferred_answer: It uses recurring automated and manual evidence to identify control drift, exceptions, and risk changes, with ownership, thresholds, validation, and tracked response.

source.title: NIST SP 800-137 - Information Security Continuous Monitoring

questions.question: What is data governance?
questions.preferred_answer: Data governance defines decision rights, ownership, policies, standards, quality, security, privacy, lifecycle, and accountability for data as an enterprise asset.

source.title: ISACA - COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology

questions.question: What is data classification?
questions.preferred_answer: Classification assigns data categories based on sensitivity, criticality, legal obligations, and business value so handling and protection requirements can be applied consistently.

source.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 - Information Security Management Systems

questions.question: What is a data owner?
questions.preferred_answer: A data owner is accountable for business use, classification, quality, access rules, retention, sharing, and risk decisions for a defined data domain.

source.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 - Information Security Management Systems

questions.question: What is data minimization?
questions.preferred_answer: Collect and process only personal data that is adequate, relevant, and necessary for the defined purpose, and avoid retaining or exposing unnecessary fields.

source.title: European Union - General Data Protection Regulation

questions.question: What is purpose limitation?
questions.preferred_answer: Personal data should be collected for specified, explicit, legitimate purposes and not reused incompatibly without a valid legal basis and appropriate transparency.

source.title: European Union - General Data Protection Regulation

questions.question: What is a record of processing activities?
questions.preferred_answer: A ROPA documents processing purposes, data categories, subjects, recipients, transfers, retention, security measures, and responsible parties to support accountability.

source.title: European Union - General Data Protection Regulation

questions.question: What is a data protection impact assessment?
questions.preferred_answer: A DPIA assesses necessity, proportionality, risks to individuals, safeguards, residual risk, consultation, and approvals for processing likely to create high privacy risk.

source.title: ICO - Data Protection Impact Assessments

questions.question: What is privacy by design and by default?
questions.preferred_answer: Embed privacy into architecture and processes from the start, and configure defaults to process only data necessary for each purpose, with lifecycle controls and demonstrable accountability.

source.title: European Union - General Data Protection Regulation

questions.question: How should consent be governed?
questions.preferred_answer: Consent must be informed, specific, freely given, unambiguous, recorded, easy to withdraw, separated from unnecessary terms, and refreshed when purpose or conditions change.

source.title: European Union - General Data Protection Regulation

questions.question: What is data retention governance?
questions.preferred_answer: Define legal and business retention periods, owners, triggers, legal holds, storage locations, deletion methods, exceptions, and evidence that disposal occurs across primary and backup systems.

source.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 - Information Security Management Systems

questions.question: How should data deletion be audited?
questions.preferred_answer: Test approved schedules, trigger dates, system coverage, deletion jobs, exceptions, backups, legal holds, third parties, validation reports, and evidence that inaccessible data is not still usable.

source.title: European Union - General Data Protection Regulation

questions.question: What is a data lineage control?
questions.preferred_answer: Lineage documents data origin, transformations, movement, storage, and use so accuracy, ownership, impact analysis, privacy, and reporting can be validated.

source.title: ISACA - COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology

questions.question: How should cross-border data transfers be governed?
questions.preferred_answer: Identify transfers, destinations, legal mechanisms, transfer assessments, contractual terms, security measures, onward transfers, and changes in law or provider location.

source.title: European Data Protection Board - Guidelines

questions.question: What is privacy risk?
questions.preferred_answer: Privacy risk concerns adverse effects on individuals arising from data processing, distinct from but related to organizational compliance, security, and reputational risk.

source.title: NIST Privacy Framework

questions.question: How should privacy incidents be managed?
questions.preferred_answer: Contain and investigate the event, assess data and individuals affected, legal notification thresholds and deadlines, preserve evidence, communicate appropriately, remediate causes, and document decisions.

source.title: HHS - Breach Notification Rule

questions.question: What evidence supports data-governance effectiveness?
questions.preferred_answer: Evidence includes authoritative inventories, ownership, classification, access rules, quality metrics, lineage, retention execution, issue resolution, privacy assessments, and governance decisions.

source.title: ISACA - COBIT 2019 Framework: Introduction and Methodology

questions.question: What is third-party risk management?
questions.preferred_answer: TPRM manages risks from suppliers, service providers, contractors, partners, and subcontractors through selection, contracting, monitoring, change, incident response, and exit.

source.title: NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1 - Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management

questions.question: What should vendor risk tiering consider?
questions.preferred_answer: Consider service criticality, data access, connectivity, concentration, substitutability, geography, regulatory impact, transaction volume, financial dependency, and potential harm.

source.title: NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1 - Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management

questions.question: What is due diligence before onboarding a vendor?
questions.preferred_answer: Evaluate capability, financial and operational resilience, security and privacy controls, compliance, legal history, subcontractors, architecture, evidence, and ability to meet contractual requirements.

source.title: NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1 - Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management

questions.question: What security clauses belong in vendor contracts?
questions.preferred_answer: Define control requirements, data use, access, breach notification, audit rights, subcontractors, locations, retention, deletion, resilience, vulnerability handling, evidence, remediation, and termination assistance.

source.title: NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1 - Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management

questions.question: What is concentration risk?
questions.preferred_answer: Concentration risk arises when many critical services depend on one provider, region, technology, or subcontractor, creating correlated failure and weak exit options.

source.title: NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1 - Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management

questions.question: How should fourth-party risk be managed?
questions.preferred_answer: Require visibility and contractual governance of critical subcontractors, assess material dependencies, define notification and approval rights, and include them in monitoring, incident, and exit planning.

source.title: NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1 - Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management

questions.question: What is vendor continuous monitoring?
questions.preferred_answer: It combines periodic reassessment with ongoing signals such as incidents, control reports, vulnerability exposure, financial changes, regulatory events, service performance, and material subcontractor changes.

source.title: NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1 - Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management

questions.question: How should a SOC 2 report be reviewed?
questions.preferred_answer: Evaluate opinion, scope, services, system description, criteria, period, tests and exceptions, subservice method, complementary user controls, subsequent events, and relevance to your risks.

source.title: AICPA & CIMA - SOC for Service Organizations

questions.question: What are complementary user entity controls?
questions.preferred_answer: CUECs are controls the service organization assumes customers will implement. The customer must identify, assign, operate, and test relevant CUECs before relying on the report.

source.title: AICPA & CIMA - SOC for Service Organizations

questions.question: What is a bridge letter?
questions.preferred_answer: A bridge letter covers the period after a SOC report date and describes material changes or incidents. It provides limited management representation, not an independent audit opinion.

source.title: AICPA & CIMA - SOC for Service Organizations

questions.question: How do you handle a vendor without a SOC or certification?
questions.preferred_answer: Use alternative evidence such as targeted questionnaires, independent assessments, test results, policies, architecture reviews, contract controls, onsite review, and enhanced monitoring based on risk.

source.title: NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1 - Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management

questions.question: What is an exit strategy for a critical provider?
questions.preferred_answer: It defines triggers, data return and deletion, transition support, replacement options, credentials, configurations, records, continuity, costs, responsibilities, and testing of portability.

source.title: NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1 - Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management

questions.question: How should vendor incidents be governed?
questions.preferred_answer: Require rapid notification, joint response roles, evidence access, impact assessment, regulatory coordination, containment, customer communication, root-cause analysis, and corrective-action validation.

source.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 - Incident Response

questions.question: What is software supply-chain risk?
questions.preferred_answer: It includes compromised components, build systems, repositories, dependencies, updates, vendors, and provenance. Controls cover inventory, secure development, signing, verification, monitoring, and response.

source.title: NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1 - Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management

questions.question: How should vendor exceptions be approved?
questions.preferred_answer: Document unmet requirements, exposure, compensating controls, business need, owner, duration, monitoring, contractual actions, and approval by authorized risk owners.

source.title: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 - Risk Management Framework

questions.question: How do you audit TPRM effectiveness?
questions.preferred_answer: Test inventory completeness, tiering, due diligence, contract requirements, reassessments, issue tracking, monitoring, incidents, fourth parties, and offboarding across representative vendors.

source.title: ISACA - IT Audit Resources and ITAF

questions.question: What is a compliance obligation register?
questions.preferred_answer: It inventories applicable laws, regulations, contracts, standards, and commitments, with scope, owners, requirements, mapped controls, evidence, deadlines, and change monitoring.

source.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 - Information Security Management Systems

questions.question: How is compliance different from risk management?
questions.preferred_answer: Compliance addresses mandatory or committed requirements; risk management addresses uncertainty affecting objectives. A compliant organization can still face unacceptable risk, and risk decisions cannot override law.

source.title: ISO 31000 - Risk Management

questions.question: What is regulatory change management?
questions.preferred_answer: It identifies changes, assesses applicability and impact, assigns owners, updates controls and documents, trains affected people, tests implementation, and retains evidence by required dates.

source.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 - Information Security Management Systems

questions.question: What is SOX Section 404 focused on?
questions.preferred_answer: It requires management assessment and, where applicable, auditor attestation regarding the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting using a suitable control framework.

source.title: SEC - Management Report on Internal Control over Financial Reporting

questions.question: What are financially relevant ITGCs?
questions.preferred_answer: They are IT controls over systems that support material financial reporting, especially access, change, operations, interfaces, reports, and related system dependencies.

source.title: PCAOB AS 2201 - Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

questions.question: What is a significant deficiency versus material weakness?
questions.preferred_answer: Both are control deficiencies; a material weakness creates a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement will not be prevented or detected timely, while a significant deficiency is less severe but merits governance attention.

source.title: PCAOB AS 2201 - Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

questions.question: What is PCI DSS scope?
questions.preferred_answer: It includes people, processes, and technologies that store, process, transmit cardholder data or can affect the security of the cardholder data environment, unless properly segmented and validated.

source.title: PCI Security Standards Council - PCI DSS v4.0.1

questions.question: What is a PCI compensating control?
questions.preferred_answer: It is an alternative that meets the intent and rigor of the original requirement, provides similar defense, addresses added risk, and is documented and validated under PCI criteria.

source.title: PCI Security Standards Council - PCI DSS v4.0.1

questions.question: What are GDPR accountability expectations?
questions.preferred_answer: Organizations must be able to demonstrate lawful, fair, transparent, secure, and purpose-limited processing through governance, records, assessments, contracts, controls, and evidence.

source.title: European Union - General Data Protection Regulation

questions.question: What is a personal data breach under GDPR?
questions.preferred_answer: It is a security breach leading to accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorized disclosure of, or access to personal data.

source.title: European Union - General Data Protection Regulation

questions.question: What are HIPAA Security Rule safeguard categories?
questions.preferred_answer: The rule organizes safeguards into administrative, physical, and technical requirements for protecting electronic protected health information.

source.title: HHS - HIPAA Security Rule

questions.question: What is a HIPAA risk analysis?
questions.preferred_answer: It identifies where electronic protected health information exists, threats and vulnerabilities, current measures, likelihood and impact, risk levels, and needed responses, with ongoing updates.

source.title: HHS - HIPAA Security Rule

questions.question: How should evidence be reused across compliance frameworks?
questions.preferred_answer: Map requirements to normalized control objectives and authoritative evidence, record scope and differences, and avoid claiming equivalence where criteria, populations, periods, or assurance levels differ.

source.title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0

questions.question: What is a compliance monitoring plan?
questions.preferred_answer: It defines obligations, controls, testing frequency, owners, populations, evidence, thresholds, issue handling, reporting, and triggers for additional review.

source.title: ISO 19011 - Guidelines for Auditing Management Systems

questions.question: How should noncompliance be handled?
questions.preferred_answer: Confirm facts, contain harm, notify required parties, assess legal and business impact, preserve evidence, identify causes, remediate, validate, and document decisions without suppressing reporting.

source.title: The IIA - Global Internal Audit Standards

questions.question: What is the risk of treating certification as complete assurance?
questions.preferred_answer: Certification is limited to its scope, criteria, sampling, period, and assessor. It does not prove all risks, systems, locations, or ongoing operations are controlled.

source.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 - Information Security Management Systems

questions.category: 14. Business Continuity, Resilience and Incident Governance
questions.question: What is business continuity management?
questions.preferred_answer: BCM establishes capabilities to continue or recover prioritized products and services during disruption through governance, analysis, strategies, plans, exercises, and improvement.

source.title: ISO 22301 - Business Continuity Management Systems

questions.category: 14. Business Continuity, Resilience and Incident Governance
questions.question: What is a business impact analysis?
questions.preferred_answer: A BIA identifies critical activities, dependencies, disruption impacts over time, maximum tolerable periods, recovery priorities, resource needs, and recovery objectives.

source.title: ISO 22301 - Business Continuity Management Systems

questions.category: 14. Business Continuity, Resilience and Incident Governance
questions.question: What is recovery time objective?
questions.preferred_answer: RTO is the targeted time to restore a service or capability after disruption. It should reflect business impact and be supported by tested technology and operational plans.

source.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 - Contingency Planning Guide

questions.category: 14. Business Continuity, Resilience and Incident Governance
questions.question: What is recovery point objective?
questions.preferred_answer: RPO is the maximum targeted period of data loss measured backward from disruption. Backup and replication design must be capable of meeting it.

source.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 - Contingency Planning Guide

questions.category: 14. Business Continuity, Resilience and Incident Governance
questions.question: How do RTO and maximum tolerable downtime differ?
questions.preferred_answer: RTO is the planned restoration target; maximum tolerable downtime is the limit beyond which unacceptable impact occurs. RTO should be shorter and include time for business resumption.

source.title: ISO 22301 - Business Continuity Management Systems

questions.category: 14. Business Continuity, Resilience and Incident Governance
questions.question: What is operational resilience?
questions.preferred_answer: Operational resilience is the ability to prevent, adapt, respond, recover, and learn while continuing important services within defined impact tolerances.

source.title: ISO 22301 - Business Continuity Management Systems

questions.category: 14. Business Continuity, Resilience and Incident Governance
questions.question: What should a continuity plan contain?
questions.preferred_answer: It should define activation, roles, contacts, priorities, procedures, dependencies, alternate arrangements, communications, data and technology recovery, return to normal, and maintenance.

source.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 - Contingency Planning Guide

questions.category: 14. Business Continuity, Resilience and Incident Governance
questions.question: What is a tabletop exercise?
questions.preferred_answer: A facilitated scenario discussion tests decisions, roles, plans, assumptions, coordination, and escalation without executing full technical recovery. Actions and owners should be recorded.

source.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 - Contingency Planning Guide

questions.category: 14. Business Continuity, Resilience and Incident Governance
questions.question: What is a technical recovery test?
questions.preferred_answer: It executes restoration or failover of systems, data, networks, and dependencies in a controlled manner to measure results against RTO, RPO, integrity, and operational readiness.

source.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 - Contingency Planning Guide

questions.category: 14. Business Continuity, Resilience and Incident Governance
questions.question: How should incident response connect to GRC?
questions.preferred_answer: Incident response should use approved governance, risk criteria, legal and regulatory obligations, evidence handling, communication, third-party coordination, and lessons that update controls and risk assessments.

source.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 - Incident Response

questions.category: 14. Business Continuity, Resilience and Incident Governance
questions.question: Who should declare a major cyber incident?
questions.preferred_answer: An authorized role should declare based on defined impact and escalation criteria, with clear transfer to incident command and rapid notification of executives, legal, privacy, communications, and affected operations.

source.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 - Incident Response

questions.category: 14. Business Continuity, Resilience and Incident Governance
questions.question: What is crisis communication governance?
questions.preferred_answer: It defines decision authority, audiences, channels, approvals, frequency, factual validation, legal considerations, spokespersons, and records for internal and external communication.
